Amplias (Ampliatus)
AM-plee-us (am-plee-AY-tus)
proper noun
From the Latin Ampliatus, “enlarged” or “extended,” a common slave-name in the Roman world.

📖 Biblical Definition

Amplias — the fuller Latin form is Ampliatus — is greeted by Paul with the tender phrase “my beloved in the Lord.” The name was an ordinary one among Roman slaves and freedmen, and many believe this Amplias was a man of humble or servile station. Yet to Paul he is no nobody; he is beloved, and beloved precisely “in the Lord,” for the love that binds the church is not the affection of natural kinship or social rank but the bond of Christ that joins the meanest slave to the chief of apostles as a brother. The world reckoned such a man property; the gospel reckoned him a beloved son of God. Here is the leveling power of grace: in Christ there is neither bond nor free, and a slave in Caesar’s Rome could be dearer to Paul than any senator. The Reformed reader sees in Amplias the dignity that the gospel confers on the lowly. He held no office that we know, performed no deed Scripture records save being loved; and that is enough. The Spirit thought it worth eternal mention that one obscure believer, perhaps a bondman, was beloved in the Lord. His name reminds the church that Christ’s family is gathered from the back streets and slave-quarters as truly as from the great houses, and that to be beloved in the Lord is the highest of all titles.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome, in the KJV called Amplias, whom Paul greets as “my beloved in the Lord,” likely a man of humble or servile rank.

expand to see more

AMPLIAS, the shortened form of Ampliatus, a Christian at Rome saluted by Paul.

Greeted simply as “my beloved in the Lord” (Rom 16:8).

The name was common among Roman slaves and freedmen.

His love-bond with Paul rested in Christ, not in rank or kinship.

He shows the dignity grace confers on the lowliest believer (Rom 16:8).

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:8 — "Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord."

Gal 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

1Co 7:22 — "For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord’s freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ’s servant."

Phm 1:16 — "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is that grace dignifies the lowliest, making a slave beloved in the Lord and a brother to apostles.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Amplias is the leveling, dignifying power of the gospel. A man bearing a common slave’s name is called by an apostle “my beloved in the Lord.” The bond is not blood, rank, or sentiment but union with Christ, which joins the lowest believer to the highest as equal heirs of grace.

Rome reckoned such men chattel; heaven reckoned them sons. The single verse that names Amplias rebukes every estimate of worth drawn from station or usefulness to the world. To be beloved in the Lord is the noblest of titles, and it is freely given to the obscure. The church is gathered from slave-quarter and senate alike, and Christ owns each as His own.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Latin ampliatus means “enlarged, extended,” from amplus, ample, abundant.

expand to see more

Amplias — contracted from Latin Ampliatus, “enlarged, made ample.”

Rooted in amplus, broad, spacious, abundant.

A frequent name in Roman slave registers and inscriptions.

KJV “Amplias” differs from the slug-form “Ampliatus,” the fuller original.

“Beloved” renders the Greek agapetos, dearly loved.

Usage

"Amplias, perhaps a slave by birth, was a beloved son by the new birth."

"No higher title exists than the one Paul gave Amplias: “my beloved in the Lord.”"

"The congregation learned from Amplias that grace makes brothers of bondmen and apostles alike."
